children: By Jonathan I. Shenkman

Every few decades, the political pendulum swings hard enough that clients start asking whether the rules around saving and investing are about to change. This year, wins by some Democratic Socialist candidates and the rise of democratic socialist rhetoric has plenty of high-net-worth investors asking exactly that question. It might seem particularly relevant Monday when President Donald Trump is meeting with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, one of the most prominent Democratic Socialists to gain office.

My view is that every political and economic cycle creates planning opportunities for those willing to look past the headlines. The ideas below reflect conversations I have been having with clients. While I am based in New York, the underlying concepts apply broadly to other major cities as well.
Here are five potential planning opportunities to consider:

Get estate planning at a discount. Political uncertainty tends to depress asset values before it ever depresses the underlying quality of the asset itself. That gap is where sophisticated estate planning lives.

New York City offers a useful illustration this year. Mayor Zohran Mamdani floated a 9.5% increase to the citywide property tax rate as a last resort measure to close a budget gap. It was later dropped in favor of a narrower pied-a-terre tax plan, an annual surcharge on second homes worth more than $5 million owned by people whose primary residence is elsewhere. Proposals like these are exactly the kind of catalyst that has historically caused appraisers and buyers to apply a temporary discount to a property's value because of the uncertainty hanging over it, before any tax even takes effect.

For clients who plan to hold and reinvest for the long term, that kind of temporary valuation dip is an opportunity to move appreciated assets out of a taxable estate at a lower reported value. If you are eventually going to give a property to your children regardless of the political climate, it is better to give it away, or move it into a trust, while it is temporarily worth less. That lower value means using less of your lifetime gift tax exemption.

There are a handful of estate planning tools that become quite powerful when the underlying asset is temporarily depressed. A grantor retained annuity trust, or GRAT, lets you transfer future appreciation on an asset to your children while receiving payments back for the original value of the assets plus a small interest rate set by the Internal Revenue Service.

The lower the starting value, the more upside passes to the next generation tax-free. A sale to an intentionally defective grantor trust works similarly, letting a client sell an asset to a family trust at today's depressed price while still paying the income taxes themselves, a useful way of moving wealth out of the estate. A family limited partnership can hold real estate or a business and often supports a discount for lack of control when interests are gifted to children. Clients have used periods like this to fund trusts with properties they always intended to pass down, letting the political overhang do work that would otherwise require a formal appraisal discount.

This matters even more for states like New York, since the state estate tax exemption of $7,350,000 per individual sits well below the federal exemption of $15,000,000. An estate can be entirely free of federal tax while still owing significant New York state estate tax. Furthermore, New York includes a cliff; once an estate crosses roughly 105% of the exemption amount in New York, the entire estate becomes taxable rather than just the portion above the threshold.

Buy the dip on cities themselves. For investors who remain optimistic about the long-term trajectory of major American cities, a temporary dip in real estate prices driven by political headlines can be a buying opportunity rather than a warning sign.

As an example, in the mid-1970s, New York City stood on the edge of bankruptcy and property values collapsed. Plenty of prudent people concluded the city was finished. Investors with a long horizon and the stomach to ride out a difficult decade were rewarded many times over as the city rebuilt through the 1980s and beyond. Not every dip reverses, but conclusions drawn from a temporary political mood have historically been the wrong bet when a city's underlying economic engine remains intact.

Revisit concentration risk. For much of the last decade, investors were comfortable holding a heavily concentrated position in large-cap U.S. equities, which is essentially a bet on a handful of megacap technology names. A meaningful shift in the regulatory environment, through antitrust enforcement, new taxes on buybacks, or sector specific price controls, would change the risk calculus for that concentration.

The current political environment may be a good moment for advisors to revisit true diversification with clients. This includes exploring various asset classes across industries and geographies. International equities, municipal bonds outside of politically exposed jurisdictions, and real assets all deserve a fresh look for clients who have spent years being rewarded for staying concentrated in one corner of the market.

Lock in today's tax rates. Roth conversions deserve particular attention in this environment. A political platform that depends on materially higher taxes on income, capital gains, and real estate to fund its agenda may eventually lead to tax rates that will make today's rates will look cheap in hindsight.

Converting traditional retirement assets to Roth accounts now, particularly if income is temporarily lower or equity values are depressed, locks in today's rate and makes future growth and distributions entirely tax-free. For clients in their 50s and early 60s with years before required distributions begin, this is one of the more durable planning ideas available, regardless of which political party holds power.

Realize these are cycles. None of these strategies require a client and their financial advisor to have political discussions or even to agree politically. The client only needs to recognize that political cycles, like market cycles, are a standard occurrence. The current wave of democratic socialist sentiment is unlikely to represent a permanent secular shift in how the American economy is organized.

American history rewards those who can separate a loud political moment from the durable economic engine underneath it. Advisors who help clients make that distinction are doing some of the most valuable work in our profession today.

Jonathan I. Shenkman, AIF, is the president and chief investment officer of ParkBridge Wealth Management and is based in New York. His practice addresses retirement planning, including collaborating on tax, estate, and financial planning strategies. He is the author of a children's book titled, D is for Diversification: The ABCs of Personal Finance .
